prize_parts.citation: For discoveries of the physiology of glucagon-like peptide-1 and its active forms, which made possible incretin-based therapies for type 2 diabetes and obesity.

statement.case_for: After the full first-round exchange I keep B033 alone, with Drucker, Holst and Mojsov. The scientific case has not been challenged by anyone: the chain from incretin physiology (Holst on the secretion and action of the active forms in humans), through proglucagon-derived peptide biology and receptor signalling (Drucker), to identification and synthesis of the active truncated peptide (Mojsov), and then to drugs with large independent randomized outcome trials in diabetes, obesity, and cardiovascular and renal disease, is original, mechanistically clear and mature. Six identical rankings are not evidence, and I note that every member argued the case on the merits. The chair's questions did change how I frame the choice. The achievement I am proposing is the physiology, and the citation says so while naming the therapies it made possible, so that the translational step is acknowledged without making the prize a drug-development award.
statement.case_against: The credit is the weak point and I do not think it can be settled by this committee from the supplied text. Mojsov's priority for the active GLP-1(7-36) peptide against Habener and colleagues rests partly on recalled history, which I have not verified. Knudsen is excluded because of the three-person cap, and the exclusion is a real cost: liraglutide and semaglutide are the molecules patients receive. If the committee concluded that drug development is the achievement, my trio would be the wrong one. I also see no way to add a second part without cutting this trio, and a two-part prize would deprive one of the three physiology contributors of credit that I think each has earned.

responses.point: Sandberg would not give the third slot to Knudsen, and says the Mojsov question should be treated as an open uncertainty to be checked against the record before the final ballot, not as grounds to drop her.
responses.response: I agree with both parts. Replacing Mojsov with Knudsen would reward the pharmaceutical step and leave the discovery of the active peptide unrewarded, which changes the citation. I also agree that dropping Mojsov on an unresolved dispute would be an arbitrary choice. My stated basis for keeping her is narrow: her identification and synthesis of the active truncated peptide was a distinct step that the later work depended on, whatever Habener and colleagues contributed in parallel. I hold that with some uncertainty, and I would record it as a judgement and not a finding. Where I differ from Sandberg is on the UPR, B048. I still see it as an elegant fundamental mechanism, but its medical consequences remain indirect, so it does not enter my configuration or alternatives.

responses.point: Wahren-Herlenius says Mojsov's inclusion depends on whether the committee accepts that identifying and synthesizing the active peptide was decisive for what followed, and that if Habener's claim is equal and he cannot be included, the configuration weakens. She also wants any Knudsen substitution made explicitly.
responses.response: This is the right test and I accept it. My answer is that the peptide identification was decisive for the field because it defined which molecule was the biologically active incretin, and that is what Holst's human physiology and Drucker's receptor and proglucagon work then built on. If Habener's claim were judged equal, the three-name cap would leave the configuration open to challenge, and I would then rather say so in the record than quietly swap names. That is an acknowledged weakness, not a reason to change the preferred configuration. I agree with her that a Knudsen substitution must be an explicit choice with a different citation. I do not make it, because it would shift the prize from discovery to development.

responses.point: Perlmann argues that CAR-T is the main alternative with June and Sadelain only, and that the committee should be candid that the configuration is incomplete if Eshhar's chimeric receptor concept cannot be credited.
responses.response: I agree and I have moved a little on how much weight this deserves. Eshhar's chimeric receptor concept is the earliest part of the invention, and June and Sadelain best represent the design and clinical translation that created the modality. Rosenberg's adoptive cell therapy and TIL work is a distinct line and I keep him out. The gap makes B026 a weaker preferred part than GLP-1 but not unfit for 2026, provided the citation is honest about what it credits. For that reason it is my first alternative, and I would not support B026 as a second part alongside B033, because the three-person cap would cut the GLP-1 trio to one name.

responses.point: Linnarsson keeps BCR-ABL inhibition (B032) as an alternative for its decades of survival data, and says the missing Eshhar credit weakens B026 more than I indicated, which is why he ranks it third.
responses.response: Linnarsson's point on Eshhar is fair, and I have tried to answer it in my reply to Perlmann: it lowers B026 relative to GLP-1 but not below the other alternatives. On B032 I accept the maturity and clinical clarity, but the principle that an oncogenic kinase is a drug target rests on BCR-ABL and Philadelphia chromosome work outside Lydon, Druker and Sawyers. It reads more as rational drug design and clinical proof than a separate discovery. I therefore do not move it into my alternatives, though I would not oppose it if the committee wanted a second achievement in a future year.

responses.point: El Manira holds optogenetics (B007) third and would back Deisseroth, Nagel and Hegemann, while accepting that six credited names cannot fit into three and that clinical translation is early.
responses.response: We are close. I keep B007 as my second alternative because it is original and has transformed causal tests of circuit function. I do not raise it to a preferred part. It is a method with only early retinal translation, and any trio of Deisseroth, Nagel and Hegemann excludes Bamberg, Boyden and Miesenböck on grounds that priority alone does not settle. Were it taken up, the citation would have to state why a tool belongs under Physiology or Medicine and accept that the exclusions are a judgement. I did not change my view on this after round 1.

uncertainties: Whether the committee will accept my judgement that Mojsov's identification and synthesis of the active peptide is distinct enough to credit when Habener is outside the three names.
Whether translation should be rewarded alongside physiology, which would force an explicit choice between Knudsen and one of the three basic-science names.
Whether a two-part prize is worth cutting the GLP-1 part to fewer than three names. I do not think so, and no member has proposed a second part in a form I would support.
My knowledge of the priority histories (Mojsov and Habener, Eshhar for CAR-T, earlier TNF and oncogene work) comes from memory and is not verified against the supplied nominations.
statement.conflict_note: No change to my round-1 disclosure. I am a frequent co-author with fellow member Perlmann on dopamine neuron topics and was a postdoctoral fellow with Paul Greengard. Neither involves Drucker, Holst, Mojsov, Knudsen, June, Sadelain, Rosenberg or the B007 names, and I see no recusal ground. Shared Karolinska Institutet affiliation is not treated as a conflict.
